title: Cross-Session Continuity and Ground Truth for an Export-Batching Fix
description: Tests the ability to reason about what should persist across sessions versus what should be freshly re-derived, why GitHub's live state is the ground truth a session must be checked against, and how a resumed follow-up session should behave differently from a brand-new one.

scenario.background: Maya files an issue: the /export endpoint times out on large datasets, so it should be batched into chunks of 500 rows, touching only export/service.py and its tests. A coding-agent session picks it up, and a second session later needs to add a follow-up fix while an unrelated PR merges a change to a shared dependency in between.

characters.name: Maya Torres
characters.concern: Wants her follow-up comment addressed without the agent re-deriving a whole new, possibly divergent plan.

characters.name: Jordan Lee
characters.concern: Worried that a long-running session could go stale relative to what actually merges into the base branch.

questions.stem: Once session 1 finishes, why is the durable state of the task the Git commits, the PR description, and the plan artifact, rather than anything held in the session's own memory?
options: Because the session's compute environment is discarded when it ends, so anything the session decided is only durable if it was written into Git/GitHub, which then becomes the single source of ground truth for what happened
Because Git and GitHub are simply required by policy, with no functional reason
Because the session's own memory is actually more reliable than what's committed to Git
Because storing state in Git avoids the need for any review of the plan or diff
questions.explanation: A is correct because a session's compute environment is discarded once it ends — anything the session decided only persists if it was committed to Git or written into GitHub (the PR, its comments, the plan artifact) — which is exactly why GitHub's live state functions as the ground truth that any later session, or a human, can check against. B dismisses a real functional reason as mere policy. C inverts the actual reliability relationship — durable, committed state outlives an ephemeral session's memory. D confuses durable storage with skipping review, which are unrelated concerns.

questions.stem: When Maya leaves a follow-up comment asking for zero-row handling, what should happen instead of triggering a brand-new session with no context?
options: The platform resumes on the same branch — session 2 reads the existing commits and PR thread as its starting point and adds the zero-row handling as one more commit, rather than re-deriving the whole plan from scratch
A brand-new session should always start fresh regardless of existing context, to avoid any risk of carrying over a stale assumption
The follow-up should be handled entirely manually by a human, bypassing the agent
Session 2 should ignore the existing PR and open a second, separate PR for the same fix
questions.explanation: A is correct because resuming on the same branch, reading the existing commits and PR thread as context, lets session 2 add the requested change as one more commit instead of re-deriving a whole new plan that could diverge from what's already been reviewed and partially approved — this is what keeps the follow-up focused and consistent with what came before. B discards useful, already-reviewed context for no benefit and risks producing a second, inconsistent implementation. C bypasses the agent for a task well within its scope. D creates duplicate, conflicting work products for what should be one continuous change.

questions.stem: Because session 2 gets a freshly-seeded environment (not a reused one from session 1), what does this correctly ensure regarding the unrelated db/connection.py change merged in between sessions?
options: Session 2's test run reflects current reality, picking up the db/connection.py change now merged into the base branch, rather than testing against session 1's now-stale snapshot
Session 2 ignores the db/connection.py change entirely, since it's unrelated to the export fix
Session 2 reverts the db/connection.py change to avoid any interference
Fresh environment seeding has no bearing on which changes a session's test run reflects
questions.explanation: A is correct because a fresh environment snapshot at the start of session 2 picks up whatever is currently on the base branch, including the unrelated db/connection.py change — meaning session 2's own test pass reflects current reality rather than a stale view from session 1's earlier snapshot. B is wrong because the change, while unrelated in origin, still affects the same dependency the export service uses, and a correct test run needs to reflect it. C is an unjustified and unrelated action outside the scope of this task. D is wrong — fresh seeding is precisely what determines whether a session's internal test results are trustworthy against the current base branch.

questions.stem: Jordan is worried about a hypothetical single very long-running session spanning both changes without a fresh environment seed in between. Why would the real CI run against current main matter more than that session's own internal test result in that case?
options: Because a session's internal test pass, run against a stale snapshot, could stay green even though the code no longer matches what's actually on the base branch — the real CI run against current main is the check that reflects the actual, current state
The session's internal test result is always more trustworthy than CI, since it runs closer to the code changes
CI and the session's internal test are functionally identical and either one is sufficient
This scenario only matters for very large codebases, not for a single-service change like this
questions.explanation: A is correct because a long-running session without a fresh environment seed risks its internal test pass staying green against an outdated view of dependencies, even as the real base branch moves on — the actual CI run, executed against current main, is the check that reflects present reality and is therefore the one that matters. B inverts the actual risk — a stale internal session view is exactly the failure mode being described. C incorrectly equates a potentially-stale internal check with an independently-run, current CI check. D understates the risk — staleness relative to a shared dependency can affect any codebase size, not just large ones.

keyLearnings: A session's compute environment is discarded when it ends — only what's committed to Git and GitHub persists, which is why GitHub's live state functions as the single ground truth.
A follow-up request should resume on the same branch and build on existing reviewed context, rather than triggering a brand-new session that could re-derive a divergent plan.
A freshly-seeded environment for each new session is what ensures its test results reflect current reality, including unrelated changes merged in between sessions.
A long-running session's own internal test pass can go stale relative to the actual base branch — the real CI run against current main is the check that reflects present reality.
